steps.body: Once data is plotted, describe its **shape** in plain words: where dots **cluster** (bunch up), where there are **gaps** (empty values), which values **peak** (tallest stack), and whether any point sits far from the rest (an **outlier**). The plot 1,2,2,3,3,3,4,4,5 peaks at 3 and falls away evenly on both sides — roughly **symmetric**.

widget.prompt: Build a dot plot of these test scores: one 1, three 2s, five 3s, three 4s, one 5.
widget.successFeedback: A symmetric mound: most values in the middle, tailing off evenly. Shape is the first thing to read from data — before any average, ask whether the pile is symmetric, skewed, or split in two.
widget.partialFeedback: Not the right pile yet. Count the dots at each value: 1, 3, 5, 3, 1.

cml.actionGoal: Build and inspect a distribution while coordinating individual values, frequency, center, spread, and shape.

predict.prompt: One 1, three 2s, five 3s, three 4s, one 5. Once these are plotted, the shape will be…

options.label: Symmetric, piled up in the middle
Clustered at the low end with a long tail
Spread evenly across all five values

predict.reveal: Symmetric — counts of 1, 3, 5, 3, 1, peaking at 3 and falling away evenly on both sides. Shape is the fastest thing a plot gives you: the balance point is visible here before a single mean is calculated.

explanationVariants: Around the peak at 3, the plot has 1+2 = 3 dots below and 2+1 = 3 dots above — balanced on both sides: symmetric.
A symmetric shape mirrors around its peak; this one does, dot for dot.

widget.prompt: The dataset 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5 peaks at 3, with 3 values below the peak and 3 above. What's its shape?

options.label: Roughly symmetric around 3
options.feedback: Right — equal weight on both sides of the peak is the mark of symmetry.

options.label: Right-skewed toward 5
options.feedback: Reaching 5 doesn't skew it — the LOW side reaches down to 1 equally far. Both sides mirror: symmetric.

options.label: No recognizable shape
options.feedback: Every plotted data set has a describable shape — this one balances around its peak: symmetric.

hints: Compare the two sides of the peak.

steps.body: Not all data balances. The plot of 1,1,1,2,2,3,4,8 **clusters** at the low end (five dots at 1-2), then trails off — with a **gap** from 5 through 7 and a lone dot at 8 sitting far from the pack: an **outlier**. Naming cluster, gap, and outlier tells the data's story before any number is computed.

explanationVariants: The value 8 sits beyond a three-value gap from the rest — a textbook outlier.
An outlier is separated from the pack; the gap from 5-7 isolates the 8.

widget.prompt: In the dataset 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 8 — what is the 8?

options.label: An outlier beyond the main cluster
options.feedback: Right — the empty stretch from 5 to 7 isolates the 8 from the low cluster.

options.label: The peak of the distribution
options.feedback: The peak is the most COMMON value (1, with three dots), not the largest. The lone 8 is an outlier.

options.label: An error to remove from the data
options.feedback: Outliers are real data unless proven mistaken — maybe one student really does have 8 pets. Name it, don't erase it.

hints: Where does the data bunch, and what sits apart?
The cluster is at 1-2; then a gap.

widget.prompt: Match each plotted data set to the shape description that fits it.

right.label: Clustered low with a gap and a high outlier
Peak in the middle with matching small stacks at both ends

pairErrors.feedback: That set piles up at 1-2 and trails to a lone 8 — clustered-with-outlier, not symmetric.
That set has no gap and no isolated point — it mirrors around its peak at 3.

widget.missFeedback: Sketch each mentally: where's the peak, is there a gap, does anything sit alone?
widget.successFeedback: Matched — peak position, gaps, and outliers pin down each shape.

explanationVariants: Five of the eight dots sit at just 1 and 2 — that bunching is the cluster.
A cluster is where dots crowd together; here it's the low values.

widget.prompt: In 1,1,1,2,2,3,4,8 — how many data values sit in the low cluster at 1 and 2?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 counts the distinct VALUES (1 and 2), not the data points at them. Count all dots there: three 1s + two 2s = 5.
8 is the whole data set. The cluster question asks only about the dots at 1 and 2: 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Three 1s and two 2s: 5 values in the cluster.

hints: Most dots at 0-1; empty 3-5; one dot at 6.
Pick the description hitting all three features.
explanationVariants: The data crowds at 0-1 (peak at 0), shows nothing from 3 through 5, and has a single distant 6 — cluster + gap + outlier.
All three named features appear: a low cluster, a gap, and one outlier.

widget.prompt: Absences this month: 0,0,0,1,1,2,6. Which description tells the full story?

options.label: Cluster at 0–1, gap, and outlier at 6
options.feedback: Right — most students missed 0-1 days, and one student's 6 sits alone past a gap.

options.label: Symmetric distribution around 3
options.feedback: Nothing sits AT 3 — and six of seven values crowd at 0-2 while one sits at 6. That's a cluster with an outlier, not symmetry.

options.label: Even distribution from 0 to 6
options.feedback: The dots aren't even — they pile at 0-1, vanish from 3-5, and one appears at 6. Cluster, gap, outlier.

takeaways: Describe plots with four words: peak (tallest), cluster (bunching), gap (empty), outlier (isolated).
Symmetric data mirrors around its peak; skewed data trails off to one side.
Outliers are real data — name them, don't erase them.
steps.teaser: next chapter: putting numbers on the center — mean and median.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Peak = most common, outlier = far from the pack.** In 2,2,2,3,9: the peak is at 2 (three dots), and the 9 sits alone past a gap — an outlier.

explanationVariants: The value 2 has the tallest stack (three dots) — that's the peak.
Peak means most common, not largest.

widget.prompt: In the data 2, 2, 2, 3, 9 — at which value is the peak?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 is the LARGEST value (and an outlier) — the peak is the most COMMON: 2, with three dots.
3 appears once. The tallest stack is at 2 (three times): the peak is 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 2 appears three times — the tallest stack, so the peak.
